chapter: First jobs and New Orleans players
title: Ear versus reading music, and the blind
summary: He argues both reading and a trained ear matter, comparing musicians to blind people who rely on hearing.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: But do you think it's good to be able to read first?

Well, both of them is good. And if you can read and don't have a ear's voice, but we call that a wooden ear. A lot of fellas that can read, but they can't get nothing up in their head. A note, they never know. It's something for us hard, they don't know when they tune up. But if you train that ear, that ear is very important. It's more important, I think, to some extent than what the eye are, because I've worked around the blind, and I find out that they use that ear. It's very important. A man with his sight, he really don't know how important that the ear is all.

We've got quite a number of people that they depend upon the ear, especially when they're blind, the ear and the feeling, and they can tell when they get to a red light, and they be looking for the ticking in that box. And the motor and the sound of the cars stop, and they can observe that. And I work around them, and I ask them different questions, and like that I know it. Even now, when they be walking on the street, they use that stick, where they get a landmark as a guy. Then you can come up to one of them and touch him, and you can know him if you don't say nothing, well, he's in suspense. But the minute you speak, well, he'll know who you are. And I think music is the same way. If you use that ear, whenever you hear that sound, well, you'll know just where it goes and where it belongs, you'll have no trouble. Yeah, no trouble at all.
